The '''appeal to loyalty''' is a [[informal fallacy|logical fallacy]] committed when the premise of an argument uses a perceived need for [[loyalty]] of some sort to distract from the issue being discussed.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://home.honolulu.hawaii.edu/~pine/Book2/chap4EL-2.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041214142206/http://home.honolulu.hawaii.edu/~pine/Book2/chap4EL-2.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2004-12-14 |title=Essential Logic: Basic Reasoning Skills for the 21st Century |author=Ronald C. Pine |publisher=University of Hawaii-Honolulu }}</ref>

;Example:
:B questions A's statement of x.
:Anyone who questions A is disloyal.
:Therefore, B is wrong.

Problem: Even if B is disloyal, that doesn't mean that B is wrong, as A is not necessarily always right.
